title: 317. Functions, Graphs & Transformations: Constructing a Piecewise Pricing Function
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.concept: Constructing a Piecewise Pricing Function with a Fixed Initial Charge
questions.learningObjective: Construct a piecewise function that models a fixed initial charge plus a per-unit charge beyond a threshold.
questions.question: A parking garage charges \(5\text{ dollars}\) for the first hour and \(3\text{ dollars}\) for each additional hour. Additional fractional units are charged proportionally. Let \(x\) be the number of hours parked and \(f(x)\) the total fee. Which piecewise function models the fee?
questions.explanation:
For the first hour, the fee is constant at \(5\), so \(f(x)=5\) for \(0<x\le 1\). For \(x>1\), the fee is the first-hour charge plus \(3\text{ dollars}\) for each additional hour:
\[
f(x)=5+3(x-1).
\]
Thus option B is the correct piecewise model.
questions.hint: Write the additional charge as \(3\) times the number of hours beyond the first hour.

questions.concept: Constructing a Piecewise Pricing Function for a Phone Plan
questions.learningObjective: Construct a piecewise function for a base fee covering an initial allowance and a per-unit charge beyond the allowance.
questions.question: A phone plan costs \(20\text{ dollars}\) for the first \(100\text{ minutes}\) and \(0.10\text{ dollar}\) for each additional minute. Additional fractional units are charged proportionally. Let \(m\) be the number of minutes used and \(C(m)\) the total cost. Which piecewise function models the cost?
questions.explanation:
For \(0\le m\le 100\), the cost is the fixed \(20\text{ dollars}\). For \(m>100\), the cost is \(20\text{ dollars}\) plus \(0.10\text{ dollar}\) for each minute beyond \(100\):
\[
C(m)=20+0.10(m-100).
\]
Therefore, option B is correct.
questions.hint: The additional charge applies only to the minutes beyond \(100\).

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the cost from a piecewise delivery-fee description.
questions.question: A delivery service charges \(4\text{ dollars}\) for the first \(2\text{ kilometers}\) and \(1.50\text{ dollars}\) for each additional kilometer. Additional fractional units are charged proportionally. What is the cost for a \(5\)-kilometer delivery?
questions.explanation:
The first \(2\text{ kilometers}\) cost \(4\text{ dollars}\). The additional distance is \(5-2=3\text{ kilometers}\), which costs
\[
3(1.50)=4.50
\]
dollars. The total cost is
\[
4+4.50=8.50
\]
dollars. Therefore, option A is correct.
questions.hint: First subtract the first \(2\text{ kilometers}\), then multiply the remaining distance by \(1.50\).

questions.concept: Using a Piecewise Pricing Function for a Gym Membership
questions.learningObjective: Calculate a total fee from a piecewise pricing rule.
questions.question: A gym charges \(30\text{ dollars}\) per month for the first \(10\) visits and \(2\text{ dollars}\) for each visit beyond \(10\). What is the total cost for \(15\) visits in one month?
questions.explanation:
The first \(10\) visits cost \(30\text{ dollars}\). There are \(15-10=5\) additional visits, costing
\[
5(2)=10
\]
dollars. The total cost is
\[
30+10=40
\]
dollars. Therefore, option A is correct.
questions.hint: Charge \(2\text{ dollars}\) only for the visits beyond the first \(10\).

questions.concept: Interpreting a Parameter in a Piecewise Pricing Function
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the constant term of a piecewise pricing function as the base charge.
questions.question:
A function is defined by
\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}
8, & 0<x\le 3,\\
8+2(x-3), & x>3.
\end{cases}
\]
What does the number \(8\) represent?

options.label: A
options.text: The additional cost per unit beyond \(3\) units

options.label: B
options.text: The base charge for the first \(3\) units

questions.explanation: For \(0<x\le 3\), the function has the constant value \(8\). This means the cost for the first \(3\) units is \(8\text{ dollars}\). The coefficient \(2\) in the second piece is the additional cost per unit beyond \(3\) units. Therefore, \(8\) represents the base charge.
questions.hint: Look at the value of the function on the first interval.

questions.concept: Evaluating a Piecewise Taxi Fare Function
questions.learningObjective: Calculate a taxi fare from a piecewise function with a base fare and per-kilometer charge.
questions.question:
A taxi fare is modeled by
\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}
3, & 0<x\le 1,\\
3+2(x-1), & x>1,
\end{cases}
\]
where \(x\) is the distance in kilometers and \(f(x)\) is the fare in dollars. What is the fare for a \(4\)-kilometer ride?
questions.explanation:
Since \(4>1\), use the second piece:
\[
f(4)=3+2(4-1)=3+6=9.
\]
Therefore, the fare is \(9\text{ dollars}\), so option B is correct.

questions.learningObjective: Construct a piecewise function for a two-tier per-unit pricing structure.
questions.question: A printing service charges \(0.20\text{ dollar}\) per unit for the first \(50\) units and \(0.15\text{ dollar}\) per unit for each unit beyond \(50\). Let \(x\) be the number of units and \(f(x)\) the total cost. Which piecewise function models the cost?
questions.explanation:
For \(0\le x\le 50\), the cost is \(0.20x\). The first \(50\) units cost
\[
50(0.20)=10
\]
dollars. For \(x>50\), the cost is \(10\text{ dollars}\) plus \(0.15\text{ dollar}\) for each unit beyond \(50\):
\[
f(x)=10+0.15(x-50).
\]
Thus option B is correct.
questions.hint: Find the total cost of the first \(50\) units before writing the second piece.

questions.concept: Evaluating a Piecewise Pricing Function at a Boundary Point
questions.learningObjective: Determine the value of a piecewise pricing function at a boundary point.
questions.question:
A piecewise function is defined by
\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}
10, & 0<x\le 2,\\
10+4(x-2), & x>2.
\end{cases}
\]
What is \(f(2)\)?
questions.explanation:
At \(x=2\), the condition \(0<x\le 2\) applies, so use the first piece:
\[
f(2)=10.
\]
The second piece applies only when \(x>2\). Therefore, \(f(2)=10\), and option A is correct.
questions.hint: Check which interval includes the boundary value \(x=2\).

questions.learningObjective: Construct a piecewise function for a two-tier electricity rate.
questions.question: An electricity company charges \(0.10\text{ dollar}\) per kWh for the first \(100\text{ kWh}\) and \(0.15\text{ dollar}\) per kWh for usage beyond \(100\text{ kWh}\). Additional fractional units are charged proportionally. Let \(x\) be the number of kWh used and \(C(x)\) the total cost. Which piecewise function models the cost?
questions.explanation:
For \(0\le x\le 100\), the cost is \(0.10x\). The first \(100\text{ kWh}\) cost
\[
100(0.10)=10
\]
dollars. For \(x>100\), the cost is \(10\text{ dollars}\) plus \(0.15\text{ dollar}\) for each kWh beyond \(100\):
\[
C(x)=10+0.15(x-100).
\]
Thus option A is correct.
questions.hint: The higher rate applies only to the kWh beyond \(100\).

questions.concept: Evaluating a Water Bill Piecewise Function
questions.learningObjective: Calculate a water bill from a piecewise pricing rule with a base charge.
questions.question: A water bill is \(12\text{ dollars}\) for up to \(5\text{ m}^3\) and \(2\text{ dollars}\) for each additional cubic meter. Additional fractional units are charged proportionally. What is the bill for \(9\text{ m}^3\)?
questions.explanation:
The first \(5\text{ m}^3\) cost \(12\text{ dollars}\). The additional amount is \(9-5=4\text{ m}^3\), costing
\[
4(2)=8
\]
dollars. The total bill is
\[
12+8=20
\]
dollars. Therefore, option A is correct.
questions.hint: Charge \(2\text{ dollars}\) only for the cubic meters beyond the first \(5\).
